Shaded band: 10 to 20 sets a week, the usual target for muscle growth. Solid: direct sets (primary muscle); lighter: secondary muscles, half a set each.
Well built: it follows the training research closely.
A solid routine. The suggestions below could make it even better.
It works, but some of the changes below would help.
Several points fall short of what the research suggests. See the advice below.

Working sets are counted per muscle group each week: one set for each primary muscle and half a set for each secondary muscle. Pulling movements (rows, pulldowns, pull-ups) give no shoulder credit: the rear delt only helps there. Progress › Muscles counts primary muscles only, so it matches the direct part of these numbers. A cycle of N days is scaled to 7 days; a cycle without rest days is assumed to run 3 sessions a week (or one cycle a week from 5 days). Meta-analyses find that muscle growth rises with weekly sets, with about 10 to 20 hard sets per muscle a good target and smaller returns beyond that; strength needs less. Groups under 10 sets score lower (strength routines from 6), groups over 20 a little lower, and groups under 6 or over 25 are flagged. Large groups weigh twice as much as small ones.

A group counts as trained on a day when it gets at least 2 sets there (secondary muscles count half). Training a muscle twice a week or more beats once a week for growth, although with equal volume the difference is small. Each group with at least 6 weekly sets scores fully from twice a week, 40 points at once a week and less below that.

Each major group (chest, back, shoulders, quads, hamstrings, glutes, biceps, triceps, calves and abs) should get at least about one set a week. Position stands recommend training all major muscle groups. Large groups count double.

Push work (chest and shoulder presses, dips) is compared with pull work (rows, pull-downs, face pulls), and quad-dominant work (squats, leg presses, lunges) with hip-dominant work (deadlifts, hip hinges, leg curls). Balancing opposing muscle groups is a common guideline, and the hamstring to quadriceps ratio is a classic marker of muscle balance. Ratios between 2:3 and 3:2 for push and pull, and between 1:2 and 2:1 for the legs, score fully; the score falls as the ratio moves away. These bands are a heuristic, not an exact rule.

Each working set is placed by its target reps: heavy (7 or fewer), moderate (8 to 12) or light (13 or more). Growth is similar across a wide range of loads when sets are hard, but heavy loads build more strength. The score rewards using more than one zone and having at least one heavy multi-joint lift; strength routines need it more.

Muscle protein synthesis stays raised for about 36 hours after hard training, and frequency studies spread sessions for the same muscle across the week. A conflict is a group (abs and calves aside) getting at least 4 direct sets on two training days in a row; each one costs 20 points. A cycle without rest days at 3 sessions a week is assumed to leave a day between sessions.
Adding load or reps over time (progressive overload) is the core principle of resistance training. This is the share of resistance exercises with a progression rule; 80 percent or more scores fully.

Duration is estimated from every set (about 4 seconds a rep plus 10 seconds to set up, or the prescribed time), the rest between sets and after each exercise, supersets resting once per round, and 45 seconds to change exercise. Up to 75 minutes scores fully and over 90 minutes is flagged. This is a practical heuristic, not a research threshold.

Results come from the training actually done. Over the last 4 weeks (or since the first session), finished sessions of this routine are compared with the sessions the plan expects, and logged working sets with the sets each day plans. Sessions count 60 percent and sets 40 percent.

For each exercise logged at least 3 times over at least 2 weeks in the last 8 weeks, the best estimated one-rep max (or the most reps for bodyweight work) of the latest sessions is compared with the earliest. Progressing on 70 percent of exercises scores fully.
